terms.comment: The usual sense of the word: the young men of a city or a people taken together (Lewis & Short). For the time of life, see youth (the time of being young).

terms.gloss: a youth, a young man or woman
evidence: Cic. Sen. 38: adulēscentem in quō est senīle aliquid
terms.comment: One young person, of the age of adulēscentia, about fifteen to thirty (Lewis & Short); see young. In the plural, young people.

terms.gloss: a very young man, a lad
terms.comment: The diminutive: in Terence and Cicero; Cicero calls himself adulēscentulus at twenty-seven (Or. 30). It can sound slighting, “a mere lad” (Lewis & Short).

terms.gloss: a little woman, a mere woman
terms.comment: Traupman gives it for “young lady”, but the diminutive of mulier belittles (Lewis & Short: “a little woman, mere woman”). Say adulēscēns or puella.

phrases.latin: quid enim est jūcundius senectūte stīpātā studiīs juventūtis?
phrases.english: for what is more delightful than an old age surrounded by eager young people?

phrases.latin: ut enim adulēscentem in quō est senīle aliquid, sīc senem in quō est aliquid adulēscentis probō
phrases.english: for as I like a young man who has something of the old in him, so I like an old man who has something of the young
